xo-arena Memory Lifecycle

xo::mm::DArena

The life of an arena

An arena reserves a large range of addresses up front and hands it out with a bump pointer. What it uses creeps forward continuously; what it commits — the memory actually backed by pages — can only move in whole superpages, so it advances in jumps.

  1. PHASE 1 mmap(PROT_NONE) Address range reserved. Nothing is backed yet.
  2. PHASE 2 alloc() Bump pointer creeps; commit jumps to keep ahead of it.
  3. PHASE 3 clear() Bump pointer resets. Committed memory is kept.
  4. PHASE 4 unmap() The whole range goes back to the kernel.

What the four numbers mean

    

      DArena tracks three pointers into one reserved range — lo_,
      the bump pointer free_, and the commit frontier limit_ —
      plus the end of the reservation, hi_. Every quantity above is a
      difference between two of them.
    


    

      

        
reserved()

        

          hi_ - lo_. Fixed when the arena is built: one
          mmap with no access rights. Costs address space, not memory.
          
DArena.hpp:110

        

      

      

        
committed()

        

          committed_z_. Memory actually backed by pages, moved only by
          expand() calling mprotect(PROT_READ|PROT_WRITE).
          
DArena.hpp:117 · DArena.cpp:594

        

      

      

        
allocated()

        

          free_ - lo_. Everything the bump pointer has passed over, including
          each allocation's 8-byte header and its padding up to 8-byte alignment.
          
DArena.hpp:114

        

      

      

        
used

        

          Payload only — what callers asked for. Together with the per-allocation overhead
          it makes up allocated(); the gap from there to committed()
          is available(), memory ready for the next allocation with no syscall.
          
MemorySizeInfo.hpp:47 · DArena.hpp:120

        

      

    


    
Why commit moves in jumps

    

      Each allocation asks expand() for allocated() + z1 bytes.
      If that still fits below limit_, nothing happens — the common case, and
      the reason allocation is a pointer bump. When it doesn't fit, expand()
      rounds the target up to the arena's alignment and mprotects the
      difference in one call:
    

    

      aligned_target_z = padding::with_padding(target_z, arena_align_z_)
    

    

      That alignment is the 2 MB hugepage_z_ whenever the requested arena is at
      least one superpage, and the 4 KB page size otherwise. Hence the staircase: sixteen
      2 MB treads across a 32 MB reservation. Turn the superpages off above and the same run
      climbs in 4 KB steps — so fine that the commit frontier looks continuous, which is
      exactly the trade. Superpages relieve TLB pressure, at the cost of committing up to
      2 MB before it is needed.
    


    
Clearing is not freeing

    

      clear() sets free_ = lo_ and re-establishes the guard bytes.
      It does not touch committed_z_ or limit_. Used and allocated
      collapse; the physical memory stays with the process, ready to be handed out again
      without another mprotect. Only unmap() — also what the
      destructor runs — returns the range to the kernel.
    


    

      This is a model, not a recording. The arithmetic follows the source — 8-byte alignment,
      an 8-byte header per allocation, commit targets rounded to arena_align_z_ —
      but the allocation sizes are an illustrative mix rather than a captured trace: three
      populations — small objects, buffers, the occasional big one — scaled so the mean matches
      the object-size slider. Guard bytes are off, matching the default
      guard_z_ = 0. Overhead is worth driving with that slider: at 16 KB objects the
      8-byte header and its padding come to well under a tenth of a percent of what the arena
      hands out, and at 64 B they cost more than a tenth of it. On the reservation ribbon that
      share is a stripe through the middle of the allocated block rather than a slab at its end,
      since the headers are scattered through the range and not gathered anywhere; it is held to
      a minimum of one pixel so a small share stays visible. Below roughly a pixel per allocation
      the page view stops drawing boundaries and says so, since at that point they are a grey
      wash rather than information. Something that ran out of reserve would capture
      reserve_exhausted and return null rather than growing; this run never gets
      that far.
